issues.legal_issue: A revenue officer appointed and controlled by the State, with duties attached to an office in the State administration, holds a civil post and is entitled to protection against dismissal without the required procedure.
material_facts: The respondent was appointed to a revenue office and was later suspended and dismissed from it.
The State could select and appoint the office-holder and could suspend and dismiss him; he worked under the Deputy Commissioner's supervision and control.
The office-holder collected government revenue and performed other administrative duties, including duties involving delegated government powers.
The office was filled by successive appointments and existed independently of its incumbent.
The dismissal occurred without compliance with the procedure required by Article 311(2).
issues.conclusion: The respondent held a civil post under the State and was entitled to Article 311(2) protection; the order dismissing him was properly quashed, and the State's appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 309, 310 and 311, read in context, distinguish a civil post from a defence post and from membership of a regular civil service. A post is an office or position under the State's administrative control to which duties connected with State affairs attach, and it exists apart from its holder. Whether the State and the holder have a master-servant relationship is a question of fact assessed from indicia including the State's power to appoint, suspend or dismiss, control the work, and pay remuneration, together with the circumstances as a whole. Article 311(2) protects a holder of such a post against dismissal without its required procedure. The Court distinguished Sher Singh v. State of Rajasthan and Bindu Nath v. State of Assam on their facts.

rule.if: public_office_dismissal_challenge and state_appoints_holder and duties_attached_to_state_affairs and office_exists_independently_of_holder and (state_can_suspend_or_remove_holder or state_controls_work)

predicates.public_office_dismissal_challenge: A proceeding challenges the dismissal of a person from a public office.
predicates.state_appoints_holder: The State selects and appoints the person who holds the office.
predicates.duties_attached_to_state_affairs: The office-holder performs duties connected with the affairs of the State.
predicates.office_exists_independently_of_holder: The office continues as a position distinct from the particular person who holds it.
predicates.state_can_suspend_or_remove_holder: The State has authority to suspend or dismiss the office-holder.
predicates.state_controls_work: The State supervises or controls how the office-holder performs the work.

issues.definition: When a challenged dismissal concerns a person appointed by the State to an independent office with State-related duties and the State has relevant authority over the holder or the work, the holder is entitled to procedural protection before dismissal.

issues.legal_issue: Part-time work and remuneration by commission rather than a fixed salary do not, by themselves, prevent an office under the State from being a civil post.
material_facts: The respondent was not necessarily a whole-time employee and generally received a commission on government collections, although a fixed salary could also be paid.
The office involved specific administrative and revenue duties under State supervision, and the State could appoint, suspend and dismiss its holder.
The State argued that the office was not a civil post because it did not normally carry a salary and was not full-time.
issues.conclusion: Neither the absence of a definite rate of pay nor part-time employment excludes a civil post; the respondent's office qualified in light of the full circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: In applying Articles 309, 310 and 311, the Court held that a civil post outside the regular services need not carry a definite rate of pay and may involve part-time employment. Remuneration and the other indicia of a master-servant relationship must be considered with the circumstances as a whole. The Court disapproved the contrary observation in Venkata Swamy v. Superintendent of Post Offices that a part-time employee cannot hold a civil post.

rule.if: civil_post_status_is_contested and public_office_status_involves_state_duties and state_has_employment_control and (work_is_part_time or remuneration_is_not_fixed_salary)

predicates.civil_post_status_is_contested: A proceeding disputes whether an office-holder occupies a civil post under the State.
predicates.public_office_status_involves_state_duti: The position carries duties connected with the State's administration.
predicates.state_has_employment_control: The State exercises relevant authority over appointment, supervision, suspension, or removal of the office-holder.
predicates.work_is_part_time: The office-holder is not required to work full time in the position.
predicates.remuneration_is_not_fixed_salary: The office-holder is paid by commission or another form of remuneration rather than necessarily receiving a fixed salary.

issues.definition: Where a disputed State office carries State-related duties and the State exercises employment control, part-time work or non-fixed remuneration does not prevent the office from being a civil post.
